newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER SHOWCASE-CHELSEA SEEK LEAGUE REVENGE FOR CUP DEFEATS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-CHELSEA SEEK LEAGUE REVENGE FOR CUP DEFEATS.

text.p: At halftime in the 1994 F.A. Cup final Chelsea had every right to feel pleased with themselves.

They had overcome the pre-match nerves of playing in their first major final for 23 years, they had rattled Manchester United's crossbar with a fierce drive just before the half-hour and they had outplayed their opponents in a goalless first 45 minutes.
But one hour later player-manager Glenn Hoddle and his team mates were trooping up the Wembley steps to collect their losers' medals at the end of a demoralising 4-0 defeat.

Frenchman Eric Cantona had scored twice from the penalty spot in the second half. United had added two more and Chelsea's dreams of their first major trophy since their brief "golden age" of the early 1970s were shattered.

No matter that the scoreline did Hoddle's spirited side a huge disservice. Order had been re-established: United had won the English league and cup double and Chelsea were confirmed as under-achievers who played pretty football but failed to win trophies.
Two years later and the F.A. Cup again brought the sides together, this time in a semifinal.

Chelsea were ahead by halftime courtesy of a goal from Ruud Gullit, Hoddle's understudy and currently their player-manager. Again a composed United ripped them to pieces after the interval and emerged with a 2-1 victory which took them to Wembley and, ultimately, to a second domestic double.

It is credit to the job that Hoddle and Gullit have done at Stamford Bridge that Chelsea enter Saturday's match not as clear underdogs as they were in 1994 and 1996 but, for the first time in quarter of a century, as serious contenders for the championship trophy currently in United's possession.
It is credit too to Matthew Harding, Chelsea's charismatic multi-millionaire benefactor who financed the renaissance of the west London club until his death in a helicopter accident in October.
Chelsea have always been viewed as one of England's pedigree clubs but a glance at the honours tables shows what a chasm there is between them and United in terms of trophies won.
Chelsea have conquered the championship just once -- in 1955. United have won it 10 times.
The Londoners have lifted the F.A. Cup just once -- in 1970 -- an astonishing record for a club still regarded as something of a "cup side". United have won the cup a record nine times.

Chelsea's only really outstanding feat was beating Real Madrid in the 1971 Cup Winners' Cup final with a stylish side based around the goalscoring of Peter Osgood and the goalstopping of England keeper Peter Bonetti.
Since then silverware has been in short supply at Stamford Bridge as Chelsea yo-yoed between the first and second divisions, always promising much but never fulfilling their potential.
It is an oddity of Chelsea-United fixtures that both sides thrive away from home.
United have always had the upper hand at Stamford Bridge, even in Chelsea's championship winning season of 1954-55 when they won an epic league encounter there 6-5.
The following season United triumphed 4-2 at the Bridge on their way to wrestling the trophy away from Chelsea and in 1960 they again put six past them in the capital, this time winning 6-3.
The last 10 league clashes in London have resulted in five victories for United to Chelsea's three. Last season United won 4-1.

In contrast Chelsea have an unrivalled record at Old Trafford, where they have lost only twice in the past 22 years. They won 2-1 there earlier this season to become the first team to take full points from the champions in a league match there since late 1994.

Saturday's match can hardly be described as one of the needle matches in the English programme. United's fierce rivalry is reserved for Liverpool while Chelsea's arch-enemies are London giants Tottenham and Arsenal.
Nevertheless, with London sides reasserting themselves this season after years of northern dominance, this north-south clash will be a hard-fought affair.
Gullit has brought a wealth of foreign talent to the Bridge and pretty football is not enough for the club's long-suffering fans. These days, Chelsea expects.
